blocks.text: 25.1 Relative Pronoun

The relative pronoun is the word used for ‘who’, ‘whom’, ‘whose’, and ‘which’ when those words do not introduce questions (and for ‘that’ when equivalent to ‘who’ etc.), as ‘The man who finds the gold will be rich’ and ‘You should have seen the one that got away.’ In Latin, as in English, the relative pronoun is very similar to the interrogative pronoun, which we saw in chapter 13.3; in fact the relative pronoun is identical in form to the interrogative adjective, quī, quae, quod. It is therefore declined as follows:

Ancient Case Order
25.2 Relative Clauses

A relative pronoun or adjective introduces a subordinate clause; the relative pronoun links this subordinate clause to a particular word (very often, though not always, the word just before the relative clause) in the main clause, called the antecedent. The relative pronoun agrees with the antecedent in gender and number, but it takes its case from its construction in its own (subordinate) clause. rēx quī nōs regit bonus est. ‘The king who rules us is good.’ The relative pronoun is masculine and singular because it agrees with the antecedent rēx, but nominative because it is the subject of regit. rēx quem vidēs bonus est. ‘The king whom you see is good.’ The relative pronoun is masculine and singular because it agrees with the antecedent rēx, but accusative because it is the object of vidēs. pulchrae sunt puellae quās amāmus. ‘The girls whom we love are beautiful.’ The relative pronoun is feminine and plural because it agrees with the antecedent puellae, but accusative because it is the object of amāmus. puellās quās vidēs amāmus. ‘We love the girls whom you see.’ The relative pronoun is feminine and plural because it agrees with the antecedent puellās, but accusative because it is the object of vidēs.

Notice that the relative clause in both Latin and English may come in the middle of another clause; one can identify the beginning and end of the relative clause because it begins with the relative pronoun (or with a preposition that governs the relative pronoun: vīdī puellās cum quibus cucurristī ‘I saw the girls with whom you ran’) and usually ends with the first finite verb that occurs after the relative pronoun.

Notice also that the word order is often very different in English from in Latin: in translating sentences with relative clauses from Latin to English one needs to identify the main clause, translate it, and then translate the relative clause immediately after its antecedent, wherever that antecedent happens to come in the English version. It is very important to keep the relative clause intact in translation; mixing words from the relative clause with ones from the main clause will nearly always produce the wrong meaning.

In the following English sentences, find where each relative clause begins and ends; then identify each relative pronoun and its antecedent. Give the gender, number, and case that the relative pronoun would have in Latin.
The boy who is over there is my brother.
Who saw the man who stole that car?
We were talking with girls whom we didn’t know.
The man that you saw is a dentist.
Will you give it to the boy who rescued me?
The things that he said are very shocking.
He was attacked by a lion that had a very bad temper.
The person whose book you stole is my best friend!
We did not know the women with whom we were standing.
The women to whom we gave the money are not actually homeless.
Is the girl with whom we spoke a friend of yours?
The men who saved him have received medals.
We love the boys to whom we will give these mittens.
The girls who attend this school are very happy.
Did you see the girls who stole the money?
Some things that go on here really should stop.
I know the man who found it.
Martha never heard the soprano (f.) whose voice she’s trying to imitate.
Identify relative clauses and antecedents, and then translate:
deos qui nos defendunt laudabimus.
dei quos laudamus bona nobis dant.
dei quorum facta laudamus boni sunt.
deos laudant homines quibus dei bona dant.
homines cum quibus venimus boni sunt.
laudamus deas quae nobis bona dederunt.
nos defendent deae quas laudavisti.
bonae sunt deae quarum nomina laudavimus.
homines quibus deae bona dant deas laudabunt.
boni sunt dei quorum nomina laudamus.
pulchra est puella quam monuisti.
videsne puellam quae me monuit?
ubi est puella cuius pecuniam habemus?
nos non amat puella cum qua sedimus.
docuit me magister cui librum dedi.
deos qui bona nobis dederunt laudabimus.
bona nobis dabunt dei quos laudabimus.
puellam quae me amat laudavi.
Identify relative clauses and antecedents, then translate into Latin:
The enemy that we will attack is in that city.
Citizens who love the gods are happy.
Did you see the girls with whom we sat?
We loved the king who ruled us.
He praised the farmer whose sheep he bought.
They will repair the walls that defend them.
Where is the poet with whom you left (from) the town?
I shall sell the horse that you (plural) see.
The horse that I have is black.
The man to whom I gave the book is here.
Will you (singular) buy the sheep that I am selling?
The man with whom you are sitting is my father.
The boys to whom we gave your books will come tomorrow.
The farmer to whom I shall give this sheep does not have many animals.
The soldiers whose camp you will see never attack us.
25.3 Volō
The word for ‘want’ is volō, velle, voluī, –; it is irregular and conjugated as follows:

rows: volunt Infinitives: present velle, perfect voluisse, no future Participles: present volēns, gen. volentis; no perfect or future

blocks.text: Volō takes a present infinitive, like possum and like its English equivalent ‘want’: volō venīre ‘I want to come’.
Translate:
eos defendere volumus.
dixerunt se velle eos defendere.
regem oppugnare volentes illi ad urbem venerunt.
pugnabimus ut hostes discedere velint.
pugnavimus ut hostes discedere vellent.
vultisne cum eis sedere?
volesne ea relinquere?
dixit se voluisse ab oppido discedere.
volui eis pecuniam dare, sed non habui.
magistro pecuniam dederunt ut se docere vellet.
magistro pecuniam dabunt ut se docere velit.
vidistine puerum nobiscum venire volentem?
Translate into Latin:
Do you (singular) want to defend her?
He said he (same person) wanted to defend her.
He said he (different person) had wanted to attack them.
We will want to attack them.
They wanted to leave him behind.
Do you (plural) want to understand it?
He will give them money so that they will not want to attack him (same person).
He gave them money so that they would not want to attack him (same person).

1 Colloquium Harleianum 7a–e (adapted): caring for one’s writing tools (perhaps first century ad).
Tea cher: dealba tabulam tuam, sede et scribe. apices fac litterarum. in atramentum tuum aquam paucam mitte. ecce, nunc bonum est.
Child 1: porrige cannam. porrige scalpellum.
Child 2 : quod scalpellum vis?
Child 1: acutum volo.
Child 2 : acutum vis? cur?
Vocabulary

rows: dealbō, -āre, -āvī, -ātum ‘whiten’ (to make a good writing surface)
apex, apicis (m.) ‘macron’ (mark indicating a long vowel)
scalpellum, scalpellī (n.) ‘pen-knife’ (knife used for sharpening pens, a process necessary at frequent intervals when using a pen made from a reed or feather)
